turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, I... I suppose I’m here because things at work have gotten to a point where I just can't ignore what's happening anymore. I'm a mathematician, you see, and I’ve been leading this major environmental modeling contract. It's incredibly complex work, predictive algorithms, massive datasets, the kind of thing where precision is everything. But lately, well, for a while now, actually, I’m pretty sure—no, I know—that the people on that contract, the other stakeholders, they’ve been tracking my revisions. And not just tracking them, they are actively planting errors in the datasets. 

I’ll run a model, perfectly calibrated, and the next day, the variables are skewed. The code is altered. They’re doing it deliberately to make it look like I’m losing my edge, like I can’t lead the work anymore. I’ve tried explaining this, I really have. I’ve showed the logs to the junior analysts, and I’ve even tried to explain it to my wife, but they just... they don't see it. Or they refuse to see it. They keep telling me, "Oh, it’s just version-control mistakes," or "Someone just overwrote the file by accident." But you don't just 'accidentally' introduce a systematic bias into a stochastic model, doctor. It takes intent. It takes planning. And they're doing it to push me out, I just know it. It's exhausting, having to constantly double-check every single line of data just to prove I'm not the one making these so-called mistakes.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, unyielding belief that colleagues are intentionally sabotaging his work to push him out, despite his wife and junior analysts providing logical alternative explanations (version-control mistakes).

It was just the grim satisfaction of knowing I wasn't crazy, before the reality set back in that I still had to prove it to people who refuse to look at the evidence. So, no, no highs. Just a very steady, very exhausting baseline of having to protect my work and my reputation from these relentless attacks.

But this specific situation... this absolute certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions, that they are actively, deliberately planting errors in the code to make me look incompetent... that really crystallized about two months ago. 

I mean, I can trace it back to the exact week. It was right around the end of the first quarter, when we were supposed to be finalizing the predictive models for the new rollout. I had submitted my data—clean, verified, mathematically sound data—on a Thursday afternoon. And by Monday morning, when we had the review, the entire matrix was skewed. At first, I thought it was a system glitch, you know? A server error, a corrupted file during the upload process. You always want to assume the best, or at least the most logical, non-malicious explanation. So I spent that entire Monday, probably fourteen hours straight, just combing through the logs, trying to find the point of failure. 

And that's when I saw it. The timestamps. Someone had been in there on Sunday night, around 11:30 PM, making microscopic adjustments to the weighting algorithms. Just enough to throw the final projections off by a few percentage points, but not enough to trigger the automated error flags. It was surgical, doctor. Absolutely surgical. And ever since that moment, for the last two months, it's been a constant battle. I fix it, they break it. I lock the file, they find a backdoor. It's been eight weeks of this relentless, exhausting back-and-forth, and management just turns a blind eye to it all. So, yes, two months of knowing exactly what they're doing.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses an 'absolute certainty' that colleagues are deliberately planting errors in their code to make them look incompetent, which is a clear persecutory delusion.

Every action I take, every line of code I write, every security protocol I implement—it's all me. It's my logic, my reasoning, my mathematical background driving those decisions. If someone else were controlling me, they wouldn't be doing it to protect the data, would they? They'd be making me sabotage my own work, which is exactly what I'm fighting against. I am fully autonomous. I decide when I log in, I decide when I run the diagnostics, I decide when to re-verify the stochastic variables. Sometimes I decide to stay up until three in the morning because I know that's when they like to try and slip past the firewall, but that's my choice. It's a choice born of necessity, of course, because if I don't do it, no one will, but it is my choice nonetheless. 

So, no, there's no outside force pulling my strings or putting thoughts in my head. My thoughts are perfectly clear, perfectly rational, and entirely generated by my own brain. The only outside force I'm dealing with is the very real, very tangible interference from my colleagues trying to ruin my models. But my mind? My actions? Those are completely under my control. I wouldn't have survived this long in my field if they weren't.
